stories.source_title: West Africa’s new mobile money rules could change who holds deposits
stories.source_excerpt: West Africa's central bank has doubled the amount customers can hold in mobile money wallets to FCFA 4 million ($6,850), while raising monthly top-up limits and relaxing rules on how issuers manage customer funds. The changes, which take effect on November 2, could make mobile wallets more useful for small businesses and households, give fintechs more opportunities to earn from customer funds, and increase competition with banks and microfinance institutions. But allowing issuers to hold a smaller share of those funds in readily accessible deposits also raises questions about liquidity, customer protection and regulatory oversight.
stories.headline: West African Central Bank Overhauls Mobile Money Wallet Regulations
stories.dek: New policies doubling wallet limits and easing fund management rules aim to reshape digital finance across the region.
stories.body: A major regulatory shift is underway in West Africa as the central bank implements sweeping changes to digital finance. Under the updated guidelines, the maximum amount that account holders can store in mobile money wallets has doubled to FCFA 4 million, which translates to roughly $6,850. Along with this capacity increase, authorities have boosted monthly top-down limits and loosened restrictions governing how digital issuers handle consumer deposits. Set to officially take effect on November 2, these adjustments are expected to expand the utility of mobile wallets for everyday households and small-scale merchants alike. Industry watchers note that the policy could unlock fresh revenue streams for fintech operators while intensifying competition with traditional banking institutions and microfinance outfits. At the same time, TechCabal reports that permitting issuers to keep a smaller percentage of funds in liquid, easily accessible deposits introduces important discussions surrounding customer protection, overall liquidity, and supervisory oversight.

stories.body:
Public finances across sub-Saharan Africa are facing intense pressure as debt-servicing costs increasingly consume national budgets at the expense of critical social infrastructure.

According to recent findings released by the World Bank and reported by Nairametrics, interest payments on public debt now exceed government spending on health and/or education in nearly four-fifths of African nations. This heavy fiscal burden severely limits the capacity of governments to invest in human capital and public services.

The persistent challenge of high debt interest highlights the difficult trade-offs facing policymakers as they attempt to balance international financial obligations with domestic development needs. Education and healthcare sectors are frequently the hardest hit when national revenues are diverted toward debt management.

Experts note that these macroeconomic constraints hinder long-term growth and poverty reduction efforts across the region. Addressing these structural financial hurdles remains a central challenge for sustainable economic development in sub-Saharan Africa.

The structure of African football's premier tournament could be shifting once again. Patrice Motsepe, President of the Confederation of African Football (CAF), has revealed that the governing body is actively reconsidering its previous decision to stage the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) every four years, according to reports by NotJustOk.

The announcement opens up the distinct possibility of returning the tournament to its traditional two-year format. Motsepe shared this development on Friday, October 9, 2026, while addressing members of the press during a three-day CAF conference.

The potential format adjustment has captured the attention of fans, analysts, and stakeholders across the continent. AFCON's scheduling has long been a subject of debate regarding player welfare, club commitments, and tournament prestige.

As CAF continues its deliberations following the president's remarks, the football community awaits further official updates on whether the biennial schedule will make a formal return.

Motsepe's willingness to re-examine the tournament framework highlights CAF's responsiveness to ongoing discussions within the African football ecosystem regarding the best path forward for the competition.
